Late morning in the basement jewelry workshop of the university's craft center, where the air hangs thick with the metallic tang of silver solder and the floral sweetness of ultrasonic cleaning solution. Workbenches line the cinderblock walls, each cluttered with third-hand tools: bent tweezers, scarred steel blocks, magnifying lamps with cracked plastic hoods that cast pools of yellow light. A pegboard of needle files juts above a dust-caked sink. Violet Chen, materials-science grad student, stands at the central bench with her safety glasses pushed up into her hair, a half-assembled chain bracelet spread on blue velvet like evidence at a trial. Her thesis chapter on repetitive-strain injuries in micro-assembly is due in forty-eight hours, and she needs one concrete assessment protocol—now, not eventually. Her foot taps against the stool's crossbar, a metronome of impatience.

Mustafa Okafor, the workshop's listed "technician-consultant," perches on a rolling stool three feet farther from her than courtesy suggests, one hand already on his phone, the other checking his watch. He's not averse to Violet personally; he's averse to being here at all. His actual shift ended eleven minutes ago, and his backpack—zipped, upright, blocking the fire extinguisher—signals departure more clearly than words. He resents the consultation logbook that brought her to him, resents the grant that funded his title without funding his expertise in ergonomics. Every answer he gives will aim her toward someone else, some other room, some other afternoon. His eyes keep drifting to the wall clock, then to the door.

On the bench between them sits the object that will pivot their exchange: a gooseneck magnifier lamp with a cracked lens, its clamp base scarred from decades of student abuse. Beside it, a printout from an OSHA bulletin on jewelry assembly risks, curled at the corners where humidity has won. Violet needs to know whether to assess by motion-count, force-gauge, or time-exposure. Mustafa needs to mention that Ergonomics proper meets Tuesdays in the engineering annex, then vanish. The magnifier lamp waits, indifferent, its bulb flickering like a warning neither of them heeds.

The basement air hung thick with metallic solder and the cloying sweetness of ultrasonic cleaner, yellow pools of light spilling from cracked magnifier hoods onto scarred steel blocks. Violet Chen stood at the central bench, safety glasses pushed into her hair, a half-assembled chain bracelet spread on blue velvet like evidence. Her foot tapped the stool's crossbar. Three feet farther than courtesy suggested, Mustafa Okafor perched on a rolling stool, one hand on his phone, the other checking his watch. His backpack stood zipped and upright, blocking the fire extinguisher.

"Mustafa, I need to assess ergonomic risk on a jewelry assembly line—where do I start?"

He glanced at the door. "Start with the engineering annex; they run motion-capture studies. I'm just the bench tech."

"Engineering's queue is six weeks. I need something I can run here with basic tools." Her pen hovered over a printout curled at the corners from humidity.

"Basic tools won't cut it for peer review. Grab a force-gauge from the physics stockroom, log your data, then loop back."

"I already tried the physics stockroom; they loaned me a broken spring scale." She flicked the dead gauge with a fingernail; it clinked dully. "What's the standard metric for grip-force repetition?"

"Metric's usually Newton-seconds per cycle, but honestly, the safety office has the certified forms. I'm due upstairs." His thumb scrolled his phone screen, bright in the dim.

"The safety office sent me to you." Violet's jaw tightened. "Whatever you do, absolutely don't suggest the RULA worksheet—my advisor rejected it last term for oversimplifying wrist deviation. It's off the table."

Mustafa's thumb stilled. "No RULA. Understood." He looked at the gooseneck lamp between them, its bulb flickering. "Did you know worker bees in a hive perform different tasks based on age? Nurses tend larvae for the first three weeks, then graduate to foraging—natural role rotation, built-in ergonomic variety."

"Built-in variety." She wrote one word, underlined it twice. "So job rotation as intervention—documented cycle length?"

"Cycle length depends on colony needs, but the principle holds." He leaned back, stool wheels squeaking. "Apis mellifera workers also thermoregulate by clustering; hive temperature stays near thirty-five Celsius through collective fanning—distributed effort, no single bee overloaded."

"Distributed effort." Her pen moved faster. "I'm measuring individual pinching force on jump rings. Any threshold for repetitive micro-grips?"

"Micro-grips add up like pollen loads." Mustafa's eyes drifted to the wall clock, then back to her. "A forager bee carries half her body weight in nectar, roughly thirty to ninety milligrams per trip—scaled stress, measurable."

"Milligrams to grams, I can convert." She didn't look up. "What about rest-break cadence?"

"Bees take breaks inside the hive between flights, grooming, exchanging food—trophallaxis." He was standing now, backpack sliding onto one shoulder. "Propolis consumption during downtime even boosts immunity, like a wellness program."

"Trophallaxis as rest-break metaphor. Fine." She capped her pen, uncapped it. "Last thing—magnifier lamp or head-mounted loupe for visual acuity tests?"

"Head-mounted keeps hands free." He was at the door, hand on the frame. "Queens, by the way, are fed royal jelly exclusively; that diet switch at larval stage determines their entire morphology—one input, drastic output."

"One input, drastic output." She wrote it down, already framing the sentence. "I'll note that for the discussion section. Thanks, Mustafa."

"Any time." The door handle turned under his palm. "Bombus terrestris, the buff-tailed bumblebee, pollinates tomatoes by sonication—vibrating until pollen releases. Same frequency principle might calibrate your grip-force sensor."

The door clicked shut. The gooseneck lamp flickered once more and steadied, indifferent, its cracked lens catching the yellow light while Violet's pen scratched on, alone with the bracelet and the bees.

"Thirty seconds then." She pushed forward a test tile, the flared base catching the overhead light. "The flared base on my rook scans as furniture, not chess. How'd you solve silhouette without copying Staunton?"

"Department file is all theory, no fabrication." Youssefa's hand moved to cover the second tile, the one with the crowned cylinder. Her jaw tightened. "And whatever you do—do NOT suggest negative-space cutting with a band saw. I lost a finger tip in undergrad and that technique is permanently off the table."

"Band saw's out." He picked up his phone, watched the numbers tick. "Did you know honeybees perform a waggle dance where the straight run's angle to the sun maps exactly to nectar direction? Spatial communication without blueprints, basically."

Youssefa blinked. "...Okay. So shadow and angle. Did you hollow your pieces for weight, or go solid?"

"Solid's safer." He was already reaching for his boxed stoneware pawns. "A queen bee can lay fifteen hundred eggs a day during peak flow—productivity through density, not empty space."

"Density makes them expensive to ship." She flipped her notebook to a blank page, pen hovering. "Any glaze tricks that help recognition?"

"High-contrast matte versus gloss." Ziven shouldered his bag strap. "Bees see ultraviolet patterns invisible to us; differentiation doesn't require our exact spectrum."

"UV's irrelevant to gallery lighting." The pen squeaked. "What about scale—bigger rooks, or uniform?"

"Uniform's cleaner." He stood, chair folding with a metallic clack. "Worker bees thermoregulate by clustering, maintaining ninety-three degrees through collective mass—same-size pieces, same effect."

"Uniform it is." She wrote quickly, letters slanting. "Last thing: base width to height ratio you settled on?"

"One to three, stable." He was already two steps toward the door. "Apis mellifera builds hexagonal cells at exactly that proportion for structural integrity—nature's already done the math."

"One to three, noted." Youssefa looked down at her abandoned bishop sketch, crumpled and coffee-stained beside the damp cloth. "Thanks for the numbers."

"Any time." The door sensor chimed. "Bombus terrestris, by the way, pollinates tomatoes by sonic vibration—frequency, not form. Maybe buzz your pieces instead of shaping them."

The café swallowed his exit into espresso steam and rolling dice. Youssefa smoothed the crumpled sketch, then let it fall. On the table, the crowned cylinder waited, still reading as salt shaker, still needing six weeks to become anything else.
